title: Bayes' Theorem
intro: Bayes' theorem turns P(evidence | hypothesis) into P(hypothesis | evidence). It is one line of algebra with large consequences: base rates matter, and evidence updates belief by a likelihood ratio.

blocks.tex: P(H\mid E) = \frac{P(E\mid H)\,P(H)}{P(E)} = \frac{P(E\mid H)\,P(H)}{P(E\mid H)P(H) + P(E\mid H^c)P(H^c)}
blocks.caption: Bayes' theorem, with the denominator expanded by the law of total probability.

blocks.text: Read it as: posterior equals likelihood times prior, normalised. $P(H)$ is how plausible the hypothesis was before the evidence; $P(E\mid H)$ is how well the hypothesis predicts the evidence; the result is how plausible it is after.

The standard example is a diagnostic test. A test that catches 99% of cases (sensitivity) and correctly clears 95% of healthy people (specificity) sounds conclusive, but if only 1% of those tested have the condition, most positives are false: the 5% of the healthy 99% outnumber the true cases. Ignoring the base rate $P(H)$ is the base-rate fallacy, and it is not a subtle error; it is the most common mistake in reasoning about evidence.

blocks.alt: A tree starting from 10 000 people: 100 have the condition and 9 900 do not. Of the 100, 99 test positive and 1 negative; of the 9 900, 495 test positive and 9 405 negative. Of 594 positives, 99 have the condition, about 0.17.
blocks.caption: The diagnostic test as natural frequencies: most positives come from the large healthy group.

blocks.text: Dividing Bayes' theorem for $H$ by the same for $H^c$ removes the awkward denominator:

blocks.caption: Posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio.

blocks.text: Each independent piece of evidence multiplies the odds by its own likelihood ratio, so on a log scale evidence simply adds. Yesterday's posterior is today's prior.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
# A test with 99% sensitivity and 95% specificity for a condition with 1% prevalence
prev, sens, spec = 0.01, 0.99, 0.95
p_pos = sens * prev + (1 - spec) * (1 - prev)
post = sens * prev / p_pos
print(f"P(positive) = {p_pos:.4f}, P(condition | positive) = {post:.4f}")
# A second independent positive test: yesterday's posterior is today's prior
post2 = sens * post / (sens * post + (1 - spec) * (1 - post))
print(f"after two positives: {post2:.4f}")
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
N = 1_000_000
has = rng.random(N) < prev
pos = np.where(has, rng.random(N) < sens, rng.random(N) < 1 - spec)
print(f"simulated P(condition | positive) = {has[pos].mean():.4f} from {pos.sum():,} positives")
# Odds form: posterior odds = prior odds x likelihood ratio
lr = sens / (1 - spec)
odds = prev / (1 - prev) * lr
print(f"likelihood ratio {lr:.1f}; posterior odds {odds:.4f} -> probability {odds / (1 + odds):.4f}")

blocks.text: Output of the run: $P(\text{positive}) = 0.0594$ and $P(\text{condition}\mid\text{positive}) = 0.167$: only one positive in six is real. A second independent positive raises it to 0.798. Simulating a million people gives 0.164 from 59 581 positives. In odds form: the likelihood ratio is $0.99/0.05 = 19.8$, prior odds $1/99$, posterior odds $0.2$, probability $0.167$.

Applied to a parameter instead of a yes/no hypothesis, the same rule is Bayesian inference: a prior distribution, a likelihood from the data, and a posterior distribution (Bayesian Inference (#/probability/inference/bayesian-inference)).

blocks.title: A rarer condition
blocks.text: A condition has prevalence 0.1%; the test has 99% sensitivity and 99% specificity. What is $P(\text{condition}\mid\text{positive})$?

blocks.title: Two urns
blocks.text: Urn 1 has 3 red and 1 blue ball; urn 2 has 1 red and 3 blue. An urn is chosen by a fair coin and a ball drawn: it is red. What is the probability it came from urn 1?
solution: $P(1\mid\text{red}) = \frac{3/8}{3/8 + 1/8} = 3/4$. Equivalently, prior odds 1 times likelihood ratio 3 gives odds 3.

blocks.title: Evidence adds in log-odds
blocks.text: Starting from even odds, you see three independent pieces of evidence with likelihood ratios 4, 0.5 and 10. What is the final probability?
